title: Karmic tail 21-4-10 in the destiny matrix: the Oppressed Soul, an orb in the fist and balance in motion

seo.title: Karmic tail 21-4-10 “The Oppressed Soul” in the destiny matrix
seo.description: 21-4-10 is the tail of someone who tries to hold the world in a fist like an orb. A ten-second date check, and why oppressor, oppressed and runaway share one script.

short: 21-4-10 is the karmic tail that popular readings of the destiny matrix call “the Oppressed Soul” (less often “the Oppressed Spirit”, and in some lists “Wandering”). Its script goes like this. A person needs the whole world: a big cause, a wide horizon, a life that comes together as one whole. That is the entry, the World (21). To keep the whole from falling apart, they take it in their fist, the way an emperor takes the orb: rules, a plan, control — their own or someone else’s. That is the mechanism, the Emperor (4). But at the root stands the Wheel of Fortune (10), and it turns anyway. Hence the main feeling of this tail — heaviness: some carry the world on their shoulders, others live under someone else’s hand that holds it. The root task is not to hold on to the world but to hold your own balance while it turns: to find balance in motion, not above it. This is one of the most common tails — roughly one birth date in twelve. And everyone who has it has the same fourth card in the centre of the chart — more on that below.

sections.h2: Do you have the 21-4-10 tail? A ten-second check
paragraphs: You can find 21-4-10 without a calculator. It comes up if and only if the first three numbers of the matrix add up to **28, 37, 46 or 55**.

ol: **Day arcanum** — the day you were born. If it is over 22, add its digits: 23 → 5, 28 → 10, 31 → 4.
**Year arcanum** — the sum of the digits of the year. If the result is over 22, add the digits again: 1994 → 23 → 5, 1989 → 27 → 9, while 1993 → 22 stays as it is.

paragraphs: Add the three numbers and check the result:

ul: 22.12.1992: 22 + 12 + 21 = **55** → tail 21-4-10. This sum is a rarity: it occurs only on 21–22 December and 22 November in years with arcanum 21 or 22. From 1900 to 2026 there are only 22 such days.
21.11.1986: 21 + 11 + 6 = 38 → not this one (this date has the tail 6-17-11).

paragraphs: Exactly **10** gives a different tail with the same root — 3-13-10 (for example, 05.03.2000: 5 + 3 + 2). The difference is covered in the questions section.

Why it works. The bottom corner of the chart, D, is the reduced sum of the three numbers: the digits of 28, 37, 46 and 55 all add up to 10. The centre E is the same sum plus D: that gives 38, 47, 56 or 65, and all of these reduce to 11. After that there is no choice: the entry M = D + E = 10 + 11 = 21, the middle N = D + M = 10 + 21 = 31 → 4. There is no other way to 21-4-10 — this was checked by going through every day from 1900 to 2100.
The same arithmetic leads to a few facts you will rarely find elsewhere:

ul: **This is one of the most common tails.** 8.6% of birth dates from 1900 to 2025 — roughly one in twelve. Fifth place out of the 26 possible tails.

**It is becoming rarer.** Among people born in the 1930s it is one date in nine, in the 1990s one in thirteen, and since 2000 roughly one in nineteen. The tail still keeps fifth place. The reason is arithmetic: years of the 2000s have a small year arcanum, and it is harder for the day and month to bring the sum up to 28.

**There are “bumper” years and months.** The tail comes up most often in years with arcanum 21 — 1929, 1938, 1947, 1956, 1965, 1974, 1983, 1992: 41 days a year. Least often in 2000, just 9 days. Among people born in December, 10.4% have 21-4-10, in January 6.3%: the month number goes into the sum, and a December date reaches 28 more easily.
**A ten at the root almost always means this tail.** Of all dates where the bottom corner of the chart is 10, 96% give 21-4-10. The remaining 4% are 3-13-10.

**10-4-21 is the same tail read from the outside.** In this scheme there is no tail that starts with 10: the first number of a tail is always a multiple of three (3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 or 21). If you see 10, 4 and 21 on the bottom ray of your chart, you are reading the same tail from the outer corner to the centre. And for people born in October, 10-4-21 also stands on the talent line — more on that below.

paragraphs: Popular interpretations explain the name with a past-life legend, but the versions of this legend argue with each other. In one, the soul lived under oppression — in slavery, in serfdom, under a tyrant or rigid dogma — and never dared to throw off its chains. In another, the person gave up making decisions and the role of leader and let others run their fate. In a third, it is the other way round: they were a despot, set harsh rules, demanded obedience and got their way by force. None of the versions can be checked: a birth date says nothing about events of the past.

But the contradiction itself says a lot. The legends disagree about which side of power the soul stood on, and agree that there was power. Above life stood a hand that held the world in its fist — and that is the Emperor in the middle of the tail. What matters is not whose hand it was, but that without it the world seemed impossible to hold. So we read the name like this: the oppressed soul is not necessarily a victim. It is a soul that has grown used to living under a weight, its own or someone else’s, and takes it to be the condition of order.

The Russian word is more precise than it seems. Ugnetat, “to oppress”, is related to gnyot, a weight laid on top of something to keep the contents from rising. That is exactly what happens in the tail. On either side of the Emperor stand two moving cards, the dancing World and the turning Wheel, and he lays a stone on them.

The tail also has a second, rare name — “Wandering”. It too rests on a card. In Waite’s divinatory list the World has “voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place”. And for the reversed card Waite gives the opposite pole: “Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence”. In the matrix the cards are not reversed, and the tail does not make your World “reversed”. But the two poles of one card, the road and stillness, describe 21-4-10 more precisely than any legend. A person with this tail lives between a pull towards open space and a habit of pressing everything down so it doesn’t fly apart. The two popular names are the two ends of one tail: the stone and the road.

sections.h2: The dance, the throne and the wheel: how the loop works
paragraphs: This tail has an unusual composition, and you can see it in the drawings of Waite’s deck. The World and the Wheel of Fortune are related cards: in the corners of both sit the four living creatures from Ezekiel’s vision, and Waite notes this for both. In the middle of one is a figure that dances. In the middle of the other is a wheel that turns. And between them, in the middle of the tail, stands the only one of the three cards with nothing moving at its centre: the Emperor sits on a throne. The whole 21-4-10 script is an attempt to seat what by nature dances and turns.

**1. Entry: the World wants the whole.** Waite sees in the World “the perfection and end of the Cosmos”, and in the figure inside the garland “joy attained in the body”: she is dancing, with a wand in each hand. Wen calls the World “the card of synthesis”, where all four elements meet, and recalls the Gaia hypothesis: “the world itself is a living, evolving organism”. This is where the tail begins — not with fear but with scale. A person with 21-4-10 often comes into a situation from the whole. Redecorating one room turns into redoing the whole flat, a new post into restructuring the whole department, a holiday into the thought of living in another country. They see a system where others see a task, and they want everything to come together.

**2. Mechanism: the Emperor turns the world into an orb.** In Waite, the Emperor is a crowned monarch on a throne with rams’ heads, with a sceptre and a globe in his left hand: “executive and realization, the power of this world”. Wen clarifies: “The scepter or crux ansata is his sovereignty; the orb is his dominion.” The Emperor has “an iron will”, and “All is in order, under control.” This is the main transition of the tail. The living world Wen writes about becomes a golden ball in a fist. In Russian this ball has an exact name — derzhava, the orb, from derzhat, “to hold”; the same word also means a state, a great power.

In life this step looks sensible. Big things fall apart easily, so a person builds a frame: rules, schedules, a hierarchy, a plan for years ahead. Then they either hold everything themselves or look for a strong hand to hold it for them: a boss, a partner, a system, “that’s how it’s done”. Either way, somebody is now holding the world. Waite adds an important caveat to this card: the Emperor’s power is “the lordship of thought”, but “theirs is not consciously the wisdom which draws from a higher world”. The hand that holds does not know which way the wheel will turn.

**3. Root: the Wheel of Fortune — a sphinx on the rim.** In Waite, the Wheel stands “for the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe and for the flux of human life. The Sphinx is the equilibrium therein.” And then Waite makes a remark that sounds as if it had been written for this tail. Sometimes, he writes, the sphinx is shown lying on a separate pedestal above the wheel, which “defrauds the symbolism by stultifying the essential idea of **stability amidst movement**”. The sphinx does not stand above the wheel. It sits on it and keeps its balance while the wheel turns. Wen says the same in everyday language: the Wheel is “the balance or equilibrium beyond the Seeker’s immediate control”. “What goes up will come down. What hits bottom will bounce up.”

Hence the root task: to become the sphinx, not the Emperor. The tail’s mistake is exactly the pedestal that Waite considered a distortion of the symbol: an attempt to sit above the wheel, apart from it, and steer its turning from there.

**4. The wheel turns.** Sooner or later the thing happens for which the Wheel stands at the root of the tail. The market changes, the company is reorganised, the children grow up, the partner wants something different, a move becomes necessary. A frame built for the old arrangement does not bend. It cracks — or turns into a cage where everything is still under control, but nothing is alive.

In Wen, behind the Emperor there are dry, jagged rocks. “The kingdom is parched,” she writes, and this dryness is “a thirst for a different kind of sovereignty than the one the Seeker has attained”. In the same breath she recalls Midas: everything he touched turned to gold, and “gold cannot nourish”. This is an exact portrait of the tail at the end of a loop. The orb has been held on to, but the world — that living, dancing world for whose sake it all began — is not in it.

**5. Repeat.** Then comes a fork, and both roads lead to a new loop. “I held on too loosely” — and the grip gets tighter. “I’ve been crushed again” — and the person puts up with it or looks for a new strong hand. Wen calls the Wheel “the karma card” and writes that it can foreshadow “that history will repeat itself”: the past becomes the future, and there is a sense of déjà vu. That is exactly how the tail feels from the inside — the same story in new scenery.

Why does the loop hold for years? Wen describes two ways to be with the Wheel: to go with its turning or against it. Against it, she stresses, does not mean losing. Success is possible, but it takes much more willpower — like the koi fish swimming up a waterfall. The Emperor has plenty of iron will. That is why 21-4-10 often works: it is hard, it is costly, but it works. The tail holds not on failures but on the fact that the effort still pays off.
**How to tell the tail has switched on right now:**

ul: “if I let go, everything will fall apart”;
you don’t start until everything has been thought through — and the window closes;
a change in other people’s plans feels like an injustice to you personally;
you wait for permission for something you have already decided;
“I’ll put up with it, that’s how it’s done” — about an order nobody has reviewed in a long time;
you defend an arrangement that has stopped feeding you, because it is “stable”.

sections.h2: The Holder, the Subject and the Runaway: one and the same tail
paragraphs: Popular legends argue about whether a person with 21-4-10 was the oppressor or the oppressed. In life this tail has three faces, and all three rest on one conviction: **the world can only be held by a hand**. The only argument is whose.

head: The Holder
The Subject
The Runaway
rows: someone else’s: a boss, a partner, a system, parents
“if not me, everything will fall apart”
“that’s how it’s done, I just have to put up with it”
easy to deal with, dutiful, patient
free, ready to pack up and go
their own life runs to someone else’s plan
the same orb grows up in the new place

paragraphs: **The Holder** carries the world on their shoulders. They decide for everyone, because they see the whole better than others — and often they really do. But whoever holds the orb always has one hand busy: with it you can’t hug, take hold of something new or simply rest. From the outside, a support for everyone; from the inside, a prisoner of their own control.

**The Subject** puts the orb in someone else’s hands. This is the “oppressed soul” in the most literal sense: a harsh manager, a domineering partner, family rules nobody has reviewed in twenty years. They put up with it not out of weakness. There is order in someone else’s order, and that seems a fair price.

**The Runaway** drops the orb and leaves. This is “Wandering” in its dark version: a change of job, city, country — among Waite’s meanings of the World are emigration and flight. In the reversed meanings of the Emperor, Wen describes the overthrow of a crushing authority: “dominating the domineering”, “a new world order”. The Runaway’s trouble is that the orb goes along with them. In the new place they either build the same one or quickly find a new Emperor.

Often all three faces live in one person. At work, a Subject; at home, a Holder; in dreams, a Runaway. That is why the legends contradict each other: each describes one face of one and the same structure. And all three have the same way out. It is not to change the hand — to hand power over, take it away or run from it. It is to stop holding the wheel.

sections.h2: The hidden fourth card: everyone with 21-4-10 has Justice in the centre
paragraphs: The arithmetic of the tail leaves the centre of the chart only one option: E = 11. In the method, the centre is the comfort zone, the place a person comes back to in order to feel in their place. Everyone with 21-4-10 has Justice there: rules, fairness, responsibility for consequences. The numbering here is Waite’s. In some popular readings of the matrix the 11th arcanum is called Strength and the 8th Justice: that is how the cards are numbered in the Tarot de Marseille.

This centre explains why the tail is so hard to see. Waite calls the Emperor “executive”. The same word appears in his list of meanings for Justice: “Equity, rightness, probity, executive”. The tail’s mechanism and its comfort zone are made of the same material. That is why in 21-4-10 control does not feel like control; it feels like fairness. “I just want things to be fair.” “But we agreed.” For the Subject, the same centre becomes a reason to put up with things: “I agreed to it myself, so everything is right.”

Wen compares exactly these two cards, Justice and the Wheel — that is, the centre of the tail and its root. For her, Justice is “human-made balance”: decisions and their consequences “within the confined scope” of a person’s own life. The Wheel is “the balance or equilibrium beyond the Seeker’s immediate control”. On the Justice card a curtain hangs behind the seated figure, and Wen notes that it seems to be “covering or shielding the yellow light of the natural world”. A person with 21-4-10 sits in front of this curtain. They feel calm where everything has a cause, a rule and someone responsible. But the root task lies behind the curtain, where something turns by itself.

Hence the most important lesson of the tail: **the Wheel is not a court**. A turn of the wheel is neither a punishment nor a reward, not a sign that you held on badly and not proof of anyone’s guilt. For 21-4-10 this mistake is especially habitual: you want to read any change as a verdict — on yourself (“I didn’t hold on”) or on others (“they let me down”). And after a verdict, of course, you want to hold on tighter.

The numbers repeat this almost word for word. The entry of the tail is made of the root and the centre: 21 = 10 + 11. The World is the Wheel plus Justice — what turns by itself plus what a person decides. The Emperor is the sum of the World and the Wheel: 21 + 10 = 31 → 4. Order is born where the big meets the changeable. This is a play of numbers, not proof, but it is an accurate one.

sections.h2: Where else the same arcana stand in your chart
paragraphs: The arithmetic that assembles 21-4-10 also places its cards across the rest of the matrix. Here is what is the same for everyone with this tail, without exception:

head: Where in the matrix
What everyone with 21-4-10 has
rows: Start of the relationship line M–R1–R
21 · The World (it is the same point M)
Sky line (month — D — their sum), middle
10 · The Wheel of Fortune (68%) or 19 · The Sun (32%)

paragraphs: **The Emperor is not the enemy.** For almost two thirds of the people with this tail, the Emperor also stands in the social purpose — where the matrix describes a person’s role among people. And for two thirds, the planetary purpose again holds the Wheel. This is our interpretation, not the books’, but the conclusion from it matters. The card that works as a weight in the tail becomes, in the purpose, the same material in a mature form. The ability to build order does not need to be switched off. It needs to be given to people — as a support you can move on, not as a stone on top.

**A mirror in October.** If you were born in October and have 21-4-10, the talent line (month — P — K) holds the same triple in reverse order: 10-4-21. This is a different position with its own reading, but the theme is the same. The reverse is almost true too: of everyone whose talent line is 10-4-21, almost nine in ten have the 21-4-10 tail. That is partly where the frequent search “10 4 21 in the destiny matrix” comes from.

**A double 21-4-10.** If your year arcanum is 5 or 14 (for example, 1976, 1985, 1994, 2003, 2012, 2021, and earlier 1931 and 1940), your relationship line is also 21-4-10. There it is no longer a karmic tail but a relationship programme, and it should be read by the meaning of the line: an orb within the couple. But in such a chart the theme sounds louder than usual.

**Closeness also begins with the World.** The entry of the tail and the entry of the relationship line are one and the same point M. That is why, after work, the second main stage of this tail is the family.
**Age.** On the age scale the bottom corner D falls on the years 60–70, and there everyone with this tail has the Wheel. This is a rhyme of images, not a forecast.
The scenes below are sketches, not a description of everyone with this tail.

The most recognisable scene is the **perfect process**. A manager with 21-4-10 sees the work as a whole and builds a system for it: procedures, reports, checkpoints. For a year everything goes splendidly. Then the market changes, a new client arrives, a key employee leaves. The system wasn’t designed for this, and he tightens the screws: more reports, more sign-offs, everything goes through him. The team stops thinking and starts waiting for instructions, while he works for everyone and grows more and more convinced that nothing holds without him. The root version of the tail sounds different: “The market has turned. What in our system has to turn with it?”

The second scene is the **parched kingdom**. Twelve years in one place, a steady salary, clear rules, a boss who decides everything. There is no reason to leave: everything is fair and by the contract. It is just that for a long time now you haven’t wanted anything. This is the Subject, and Wen’s Midas is about them: there is gold, but it does not nourish. The root task here is not necessarily to quit. First you need to notice that the wheel turned long ago, and you are still holding yesterday’s arrangement.

The third scene is the **window that closed**. You are offered a project, a move, a partnership. The Emperor says: first work everything out. While the calculations go on, the Wheel hands the opportunity to whoever came in first. Later this is called “bad luck”, though it was a matter of speed.

In money the Wheel means waves: “What goes up will come down.” The tail wants income to be as even as a ruled line, and finds swings hard to bear. The Holder controls every expense; the Subject clings to a fixed salary for years. The lived-through version builds order not against the waves but for them: a reserve for the downturn, several sources of income, a rule decided in advance for what to do on the upswing. This is an Emperor who serves the Wheel.

Where the pairing of these cards works as a talent: managing large projects, operations, logistics, systems architecture, international projects, crisis management — anything where a structure has to survive change. The specific profession is set by interests and skills; the cards only give a direction.

For everyone with this tail, the relationship line begins with the same World. A person with 21-4-10 does not enter closeness for a while: they need a whole world for two — a shared home, a shared plan, a future in which everything has come together.

Then a **family constitution** appears in the couple — unwritten, but very detailed. Who decides about money, how weekends are spent, what counts as normal and what doesn’t. While life runs smoothly, it is a support. Then the Wheel turns: a child is born, someone loses their job, the partner wants to study, change profession, move. The constitution doesn’t change, and one of the two starts to feel like a subject.

Imagine: the partner says they want to leave a stable job and try a business of their own. The Holder answers: “We had a plan.” The Subject silently agrees and stores up resentment. The Runaway mentally packs a suitcase. The root version sounds like this: “Our plan is five years old. Let’s see what in it is still about us and what no longer is.” The Wheel has turned — so it is time to rebuild the agreements, not defend them.

The second scene is **patience under oppression**. A person lives for years with a domineering partner and calls it stability: “at least everything is clear”, “everyone’s like that”. The centre in Justice prompts: once agreed, it must be kept. But an agreement that has never once been reviewed is no longer a contract; it is a weight.

In its strong version, 21-4-10 is one of the most reliable partners for big changes. With them you can build a house, raise children, move halfway across the world, because they know how to hold the whole. The only question is whether they are holding the couple’s balance — or the couple itself.

The tail’s second popular name is “Wandering”, and it has a basis: among Waite’s meanings of the World are voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place. The theme of the road often comes up for 21-4-10, but in two opposite forms.

The first is a **dream under the weight**. For many years a person wants to live in another city or another country, but the Emperor says: “First get everything ready.” The language, money, work, housing, guarantees — the list grows faster than it gets done. The dream becomes a plan that never starts.

The second is **running away with the orb**. A person leaves abruptly to break free of someone else’s power or of their own exhaustion. A year later, in the new place, it all repeats: the same control, the same boss with a different face, the same list of rules.

In Waite, “route” and “flight” stand in one list, and that is the exact fork of this tail. A route leads to something. Flight leads away from something and takes along what you were running from. The test question for 21-4-10: am I going towards the world, or away from the throne?

A parent with 21-4-10 sees their child’s life as a whole: school, clubs, university, profession. They build a reliable frame for it and put a lot of effort into it. The difficulty comes when the child’s own wheel starts turning: interests change, plans stop matching the parents’. Then you want to hold on tighter: “I know better where this will lead.” The root version: “This is your life. My frame is there for support, not for the route.”

If a child has 21-4-10, they are often either very “easy” — living by the rules and waiting for permission — or early on become the leader in the yard and in class. Such a child benefits from rules that are explained and reviewed with them from time to time, and from experience of change in a safe dose: new places, trips, days without a schedule. There are noticeably fewer such children than in past generations: among those born since 2000, about one in nineteen has 21-4-10.

sections.h2: Support or oppression: how to tell them apart
paragraphs: The whole 21-4-10 tail rests on a few substitutions. Learn to tell them apart, and the loop loses half its power.

**Support or oppression.** Support helps you move; oppression keeps you from rising. The test is simple: what happens to your order when something changes? If it adapts, it is support. If you rush to defend it, it has already become a weight.

**A compass or rails.** A compass sets the direction and lets you change the road. Rails set the road and let you change nothing. In this tail the Emperor can be trusted with the compass: where we are going and why. On the Wheel, rails are the first thing to break.

**Responsibility or omnipotence.** Responsibility means answering for your part: for a decision, a word, the consequences. That is the zone of Justice, and in 21-4-10 it is in the centre of the chart. Omnipotence means trying to answer also for which way the wheel turns. The first makes a person reliable, the second exhausted.
**Patience or submission.** Patience has a deadline and a goal: “I’ll put up with it until the end of the project, because I want to finish it.” Submission has neither: “that’s how it’s done”.

**A route or flight.** A route leads to the world, flight away from the throne. From the outside you can’t tell them apart. The difference shows a year later: a route brings you to something new, flight to the old thing in a new place.

**Change or verdict.** A turn of the wheel does not tell you who is to blame. If your first thought after a change is “who let this happen?”, you are once again looking at the Wheel through the eyes of Justice.

sections.h2: The tail in shadow and in light
paragraphs: The words “the tail in minus” and “the tail in plus” are easier to understand as two ways of handling the same material, not as a property of the person.

head: Theme
In shadow
In light
rows: all or nothing: “I’ll take it on when I can do the whole thing”
the whole is assembled from finished parts
hold everything yourself or hand it to a strong hand
share it: what I decide, what we decide together
a verdict: someone didn’t hold on
a turn: what to do now
an escape after which everything repeats
a road on which you can change
“I go by the rules” as an excuse for control
fairness with room for the unexpected

sections.h2: What to do with the 21-4-10 tail: eight practices
paragraphs: These are the author’s exercises, derived from the logic of the triple — not a rite and not a guarantee of results.

ol: **The scales and the wheel.** When a situation worries you, divide a sheet into two columns. On the left, what depends on your decision: what to say, what to do, what to answer for. These are the scales of Justice. On the right, what will turn by itself: other people’s decisions, the market, time. This is the Wheel. Act on the left column, prepare for the right one, but don’t try to steer it. If the right column has ended up in your plan for tomorrow, you have climbed back onto the pedestal above the wheel.

**A rule with a use-by date.** Give every new rule, plan and agreement a review date: in the family, at work, in your own schedule. This is an Emperor who knows the wheel will turn and books a meeting with it in advance.

**Unclench the hand.** If you are a Holder, hand over one task entirely, not in bits, for an agreed period, and don’t redo it after the other person. If you are a Subject, make one decision completely on your own, without asking anyone’s permission. For the two faces of the tail it is the same exercise: pass the orb on or take it up, but don’t squeeze it.

**An entry date instead of a ready date.** When an opportunity appears, set not the day when everything will be ready, but the day when you go in with what you have. The Wheel hands out chances to those who went in, not to those who finished counting.

**A small whole.** Once a week, finish one small task completely, down to the last detail. The World is the card of completion. Small finished worlds feed this tail better than a big plan that waits years for ideal conditions.

**A change of place.** Once a month, a new road: a different route, an unfamiliar town, a day without a schedule. Waite lists this directly among the meanings of the World: route, change of place. A small dose of movement gets you used to the idea that turning is not dangerous.

**The sphinx’s question.** When plans collapse, replace the two habitual questions — “who is to blame?” and “why didn’t I hold on?” — with one: “Where is my balance right now, and what is the next step?” Waite’s sphinx does not stop the wheel. It sits on it.

**Find the stream.** In Wen, behind the Emperor are dry rocks, but “A small stream runs at the foot of the canyon.” Once a week, ask yourself: what in my orderly kingdom actually nourishes me? That is what to protect first — before the rules.

paragraphs: The signs that the practice is working are modest and checkable. You review agreements before they start to press. You go into things without being fully ready — and you cope. A change prompts the question “what now?”, not a search for someone to blame. Around you, people feel freer, not more cramped.

sections.h2: The strength of 21-4-10: an order you can dance in
paragraphs: In its lived-through version 21-4-10 gives a rare combination. The World lets you see the whole and carry big things through to the end. The Emperor knows how to give that whole a form that can take the load. The Wheel teaches you to keep that form in motion. Such people build houses, companies, families and projects that survive crises — because from the very start they build them with a turn in mind. They do not panic when everything changes. They know you can stay on the wheel if you hold your balance, not the rim.

In Waite’s description of the World there is a detail that fits this tail like a key. He compares the garland in which the figure dances to “a chain of flowers”. And he retells Éliphas Lévi: a chain of roses “is less easily broken than a chain of iron”. For 21-4-10 this is the formula of the way out. An order held together by agreement is stronger than an order held together by a grip. A boundary can be a garland, not bars, and inside it you can dance.

The world does not fit in a fist. But you can live in it like the figure on the last card of the Major Arcana — in motion, without a throne and without a pedestal. For that you need to hold not the world, but your balance.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: **Calculation** — Natalia Ladini’s classic destiny matrix scheme with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M; every sum over 22 is reduced by adding its digits. The “28, 37, 46 or 55” rule was checked by going through every day from 1900 to 2100. Frequencies, years, months and the constant points of the chart were calculated over all dates from 1900 to 2025.

**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922) and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Quotations are given in the original English. The numbering follows Waite: 11 is Justice, 22 is the Fool.

**The names “the Oppressed Soul”, “the Oppressed Spirit”, “Wandering” and the past-life legends** come from popular interpretations of the destiny matrix. Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the matrix or karmic tails. Assembling the three cards into a script, the three faces of the tail, reading the centre as the reason the loop holds and the sphinx as the root task are the author’s interpretation.
The destiny matrix is an esoteric model for self-observation with no scientific evidence base. This is not a forecast, not a diagnosis and not advice on health, money or relationships.

faq.q: What happened in the past life of a person with the 21-4-10 tail?
faq.a: Popular interpretations tell different stories. In one version the soul lived in slavery or under a tyrant and did not dare to free itself. In another it gave up making decisions itself and let others run its fate. In a third, on the contrary, it was a despot. These are legends of the tradition: neither numbers nor cards establish events of past lives. It is more useful to read them as a description of what can be seen right now: a habit of living as if the world rests only on someone’s hand.

In this calculation scheme a tail cannot start with 10: its first number is always a multiple of three — 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 or 21. So 10-4-21 on the bottom ray is the same 21-4-10 read from the outer corner to the centre, and it is best read in the direct order: the entry is the World, the root is the Wheel. There is also a second case. For people with 21-4-10 born in October, the triple 10-4-21 stands on the talent line. That is no longer the tail but a different position with its own meaning.

They share a root — the Wheel of Fortune — but everything else is different. 3-13-10 comes up only when the sum of the first three numbers is exactly 10, and it is rare: about one date in 309, against one in 12 for 21-4-10. Of all dates with a ten at the root, 96% give exactly 21-4-10. The entry and mechanism of 3-13-10 are different — the Empress and Death — and so is the centre: not Justice but Judgement (20). So it has a script of its own and needs to be read separately, not as a variant of this tail.

faq.q: Are the 21-4-10 tail and “the 21-4-10 programme” the same thing?
faq.a: A karmic tail is only the triple on the bottom ray of the chart, between the centre and the bottom corner. Many sites call the tail itself a programme, and then it is one and the same thing. But the same numbers can also stand on the relationship line: for people with this tail that happens when the year arcanum is 5 or 14 (for example, in 1985, 1994 or 2003). There it is a relationship programme, and it should be read by the meaning of the line.

faq.q: Does “the Oppressed Soul” mean I will be oppressed, or that I am a tyrant myself?
faq.a: No. The name is an image, not a forecast and not a description of character. The tail describes a habitual pattern: holding the whole together through control, your own or someone else’s. It can show itself very gently: in a love of plans, in difficulty delegating, in long patience with a job that stopped bringing joy long ago. Whether to be a Holder, a Subject or neither is decided each time by the person, not by the number.

faq.q: Does 21-4-10 promise a move or emigration?
faq.a: The tail does not predict events. It does have a theme of the road: among Waite’s meanings of the World are voyage, emigration and change of place, and one of the tail’s popular names is “Wandering”. But it can show up in different ways: as a dream, as a habit of changing surroundings, as a question of why you want to leave. The useful test is the same as above: are you going towards the world, or away from the throne?

faq.q: Is 21-4-10 different for women and men?
faq.a: No. Sex plays no part in the calculation, and the meaning of the tail does not depend on it. Advice you sometimes come across, like “a woman should develop softness, a man should learn not to give orders”, is stereotype, not a conclusion from the cards. The Holder, the Subject and the Runaway occur equally in everyone.

The numbers in the matrix do not change; what changes is how the script is played out. Signs of a lived-through tail: agreements are reviewed before they start to press; you go into things without ideal readiness; a change prompts the question “what now?”, not a search for someone to blame; you can both take responsibility and hand it over; people around you feel freer.

report: The legends about the 21-4-10 tail cannot agree whether the soul in a past life was a slave or a despot. In one version it lived under a tyrant and never dared to throw off its chains. In another it gave up making decisions and handed its fate to others. In a third it got its way by force. Hence its popular name, “the Oppressed Soul”. None can be checked: a birth date says nothing about past lives.

But the contradiction itself says more than any version. The legends disagree about which side of power the soul stood on, and agree that there was power: above life stood a hand that held the world in its fist. That is the Emperor, the middle of the tail. So in our reading the oppressed soul is not necessarily a victim. It is a soul used to living under a weight, its own or someone else’s, and **takes the weight to be the condition of order**. The Russian word for “oppressed” comes from gnyot, a weight laid on top to keep the contents from rising.

report.h3: Two cards in motion, one on a throne

report: In Waite’s deck the World and the Wheel of Fortune are related cards: in the corners of both sit the four living creatures from Ezekiel’s vision. In the middle of one a figure dances; in the middle of the other a wheel turns. Between them stands the only card of the three with nothing moving at its centre: the Emperor on his throne. The whole 21-4-10 script is an attempt to seat what by nature dances and turns.

It begins with scale. Waite sees in the World “the perfection and end of the Cosmos”. A person with this tail comes into a situation from the whole: redecorating one room turns into redoing the whole flat, a new post into restructuring the department, a holiday into thoughts of living abroad.

Big things fall apart easily, so the Emperor steps in. In Waite he is a monarch with a sceptre and a globe in his hand: “executive and realization, the power of this world”. The living world becomes a ball in a fist. English calls it the orb; Russian has a more exact name — **derzhava, from derzhat, “to hold”**. Rules, schedules, a plan for years ahead — one’s own or someone else’s.

report.h3: The sphinx sits on the wheel, not above it

report: At the root lies the Wheel of Fortune. In Waite it stands for “the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe”, and the sphinx on top is “the equilibrium therein”. Then Waite makes a remark that reads as if written for this tail. Sometimes, he notes, the sphinx is shown on a separate pedestal above the wheel, which “defrauds the symbolism by stultifying the essential idea of stability amidst movement”. The mistake of 21-4-10 is exactly this pedestal: to sit above the wheel and steer its turning from there.

The wheel turns anyway. The market changes, the children grow up, the partner wants something different. A frame built for the old arrangement does not bend: it cracks, or becomes a cage where everything is under control but nothing is alive. “The kingdom is parched,” Wen writes of the Emperor, and she recalls Midas: everything he touched turned to gold, and “gold cannot nourish”. The orb is held, but no living world is left in it.

Why does the loop hold for years? Going against the Wheel, Wen stresses, does not mean losing: success is possible, but it takes far more will — like the koi fish swimming up a waterfall. The Emperor has iron will to spare. **The tail holds not on failures but on the fact that the effort still pays off.**

report.h3: The only question is whose hand

report: The tail has three faces, and all rest on one conviction: the world can only be held by a hand. The Holder carries the world and decides for everyone, but whoever holds the orb always has one hand busy: it can neither hug nor take anything new. The Subject hands the orb to a harsh boss, a domineering partner, family rules nobody has reviewed in twenty years. They put up with it not out of weakness: there is order in someone else’s order.

The Runaway drops the orb and leaves. The tail’s rare second name, “Wandering”, is also written into a card: Waite’s meanings for the World include “voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place”. A route leads towards something. Flight leads away from something and takes along the very thing it runs from: in the new place the same orb grows back. The test question for 21-4-10: am I going towards the world, or away from the throne?

Often all three faces live in one person: a Subject at work, a Holder at home, a Runaway in dreams. That is why the legends argue — each describes one face. The way out is the same for all three: not to change the hand but to stop holding the wheel.

Everyone with 21-4-10 has the same fourth card in the centre of the chart, in the comfort zone: Justice (11). It explains why the tail is so hard to see. Waite calls the Emperor “executive”. The same word closes his list of meanings for Justice: “Equity, rightness, probity, executive”. The mechanism and the comfort zone are made of the same material, **so control does not feel like control — it feels like fairness**: “I just want things to be fair.” For the Subject the same centre becomes a reason to endure: “I agreed to it myself, so everything is right.”

Wen compares exactly these two cards. For her, Justice is “human-made balance”; the Wheel is “the balance or equilibrium beyond the Seeker’s immediate control”. Hence the tail’s main lesson: the Wheel is not a court. A turn is neither a punishment nor a reward, not a sign of having held on badly and not proof of anyone’s guilt. And after a verdict — “I didn’t hold on”, “they let me down” — the urge is to grip even tighter.

report.h3: A chain of roses is harder to break than iron

report: The way out is to become the sphinx, not the Emperor — to build order not against the turns but for them:

ul: a review date for every rule, plan and agreement;
setting not a ready date but an entry date, going in with what is at hand: the Wheel hands out chances to those who went in, not to those who finished counting;
when plans collapse, replacing the questions “who is to blame?” and “why didn’t I hold on?” with one: “where is my balance right now, and what is the next step?”

report: In the lived-through version the World sees the whole, the Emperor gives it a form that can take the load, and the Wheel teaches how to keep that form in motion. Such people build houses, companies and families that survive crises, because from the start they build with a turn in mind.

Waite compares the garland in which the World’s figure dances to “a chain of flowers”, and retells Éliphas Lévi: a chain of roses “is less easily broken than a chain of iron”. **An order held together by agreement is stronger than an order held together by a grip.** The world does not fit in a fist. What needs holding is not the world but balance.
